answers.l: Tony Hoare, 1959, devised while he was a visiting student in Moscow.
John von Neumann, 1945. Stable, O(n log n) worst case, and what linked lists want.
In 2007, Barack Obama told Eric Schmidt that "the bubble sort would be the wrong way to go."
Beats fancier sorts on tiny inputs, which is why hybrid sorts hand it the small runs.
Never more than n − 1 swaps. Useful when writes are expensive.
J. W. J. Williams, 1964. The same paper introduced the binary heap.
Punched-card sorting machines ran it one column at a time, decades before electronic computers.
Harold Seward, 1954. Linear time when the key range is small.
Scatter into buckets, sort each one, gather. Great on uniformly distributed keys.
Donald Shell, 1959. Its complexity depends on the gap sequence and is still open for many of them.
Insert everything into a binary search tree, then walk it in order.
Tim Peters, 2002, for CPython. Adopted by Java, Android and V8. A 2015 formal-verification effort found a bug in it.
David Musser, 1997. Quicksort that bails out to heapsort when recursion gets too deep. The usual std::sort.
Shuffle until sorted. Expected running time O(n · n!).
Bubble sort that alternates direction each pass, so small values at the end move quickly.
Orson Peters’ pattern-defeating quicksort. Go’s sort package has used it since Go 1.19.
Vladimir Yaroslavskiy, 2009. Java 7’s Arrays.sort for primitives.
Bubble sort with a shrinking gap. The magic shrink factor is about 1.3.
One loop, no nesting. First published in 2000 as "stupid sort."
Sorting by prefix reversals. Bill Gates co-wrote a 1979 paper on its bounds with Christos Papadimitriou.
Each number sleeps that many seconds, then prints itself. Posted anonymously on 4chan in 2011.
Sort the first two-thirds, the last two-thirds, then the first two-thirds again. O(n^2.71).
Named after the solitaire game. The number of piles is the longest increasing subsequence.
Writes each element straight to its final position. The minimum possible number of writes.
Ken Batcher’s 1968 sorting network. A fixed compare schedule makes it a GPU favorite.
Brick sort. Alternating compare-and-swap phases that parallelize cleanly.
Runs a knockout tournament to find each next element.
Munro and Wild, 2018. Its merge policy replaced Timsort’s in CPython 3.11.
Dijkstra, 1981. An adaptive heapsort built on Leonardo numbers.
Broder and Stolfi’s 1986 "multiply and surrender" joke, from "Pessimal Algorithms and Simplexity Analysis."
Cut a spaghetti rod per number, slam the bundle on a table, lower your hand. A. K. Dewdney, 1984.
Beads fall down abacus rods. Arulanandham, Calude and Dinneen, 2002.
Gapped insertion sort: leave space on the shelf, like a librarian. Bender, Farach-Colton and Mosteiro.
Pulls sorted sublists out of the input and merges them.
Karl-Dietrich Neubert, 1998. Guesses each item’s final position from the value range.
Stable, in place, O(n log n). Implemented as WikiSort and GrailSort.

nope.binary search: That finds things in sorted data. It doesn’t sort them.
nope.topological: That orders a graph. Save it for a graph prompt.
nope.quickselect: A close cousin. It finds the k-th element without sorting the rest.
nope.std::sort: An API. Underneath, it is usually introsort.

traps.q: Name the sorting algorithm Tony Hoare invented in 1959.
traps.l: He thought of it while working on machine translation in Moscow, to sort words before looking them up.

traps.q: Name the sort that Barack Obama said, in 2007, would be the wrong way to go.
